Winston Churchill was a British statesman, soldier and writer who was Prime Minister from 1940 to 1945, leading Britain through the Second World War, and again from 1951 to 1955. In 1940 he refused to make peace with Nazi Germany when Britain stood almost alone.

He was born at Blenheim Palace into an aristocratic family; his mother was American. As a young cavalry officer and war reporter he served in India, Sudan and South Africa, where his escape from a Boer prison made him famous. He entered Parliament in 1900 and sat there for most of the next sixty years.

A long, uneven career:

  • As a Liberal minister before 1914 he helped start state pensions and labour exchanges.
  • As First Lord of the Admiralty he backed the failed Gallipoli campaign of 1915 and lost his post.
  • As Chancellor of the Exchequer he returned Britain to the gold standard in 1925, a decision later seen as a mistake.
  • In the 1930s, out of office, he warned against Hitler and against self rule for India.

He became Prime Minister in May 1940 as Germany overran France. His speeches ("we shall fight on the beaches", "their finest hour") rallied the country through the Battle of Britain and the Blitz. He built the alliance with Franklin Roosevelt's United States and, after 1941, with Stalin's Soviet Union, and met them at Tehran and Yalta to plan the peace. His record also includes the Bengal famine of 1943 and a lasting hostility to Indian independence.

Voters turned him out in July 1945. In 1946 he warned of an "iron curtain" across Europe. He won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1953 for his histories and speeches, and was given a state funeral in 1965. See also the World Wars and Britain.
